parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ба́вити (báviti), the sense "to entertain" is probably a semantic loan from Middle Polish bawić; from Old East Slavic бавити (baviti); from Proto-Slavic *baviti. Formally, a causative of бу́ти (búty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian будынокъ (budynok), from Middle Polish budynek (“building”), from Middle High German *būding (“building, structure”). Compare Belarusian будынак (budynak).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ва́нна (vánna), from Middle Polish wanna, from German Wanne, from Latin vannus.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian ве́ресень (véresenʹ), from earlier Old Ruthenian вресень, врешень (vresenʹ, vrešenʹ), remodeled after native ве́ресъ (véres), from Middle Polish wrzesień, from Proto-Slavic *versьnь. By surface analysis, ве́рес (véres, “heather”) + -ень (-enʹ), since heather flowers in S

parole.significato: rest, relaxation (relief from exertion; state of quiet and recreation)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian отпочинокъ (otpočinok), from Middle Polish odpoczynek. Compare Belarusian адпачы́нак (adpačýnak). By surface analysis, відпочи́н- (vidpočýn-) + -ок (-ok).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian гакъ (hak) (XVI), from Middle Polish hak, from Middle High German hāke, from Old High German hāko (“hook”), from Proto-Germanic *hakô (“hook”).

parole.significato: to quench, to harden by quenching (to cool (a hot metal object) rapidly by direct contact with liquid coolant, thereby…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian гартовати (hartovati), from Middle Polish hartować, further borrowed from German härten, from hart. By surface analysis, гарт (hart) + -ува́ти (-uváty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian дꙋхове́нство (duxovénstvo), from Middle Polish duchowieństwo, a calque of German Geistlichkeit; possibly, later reborrowed from Russian духове́нство (duxovénstvo). By surface analysis, духо́вний (duxóvnyj) + -ство (-stvo).

parole.significato: to tuck up, to tuck in, to roll up (clothes: sleeves, pants, skirt, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian закасати (zakasati), from Middle Polish zakasać. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + -каса́ти (-kasáty).

parole.significato: to take into account, to consider, to pay attention to, to heed, to mind
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian зважа́ти (zvažáti), from Middle Polish zważać. By surface analysis, зва́жити (zvážyty) + -а́ти (-áty).

parole.significato: to take into account, to consider, to pay attention to, to heed, to mind (perfective aspect of зважа́ти (zvažáty))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian зва́жити (zvážiti), from Middle Polish zważyć. By surface analysis, з- (z-) + ва́жити (vážyty).

parole.significato: profit (total income or cash flow minus expenditures)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian зы́скъ (zýsk), from Middle Polish zysk, possibly later reborrowed from Polish zysk. Deverbal from зиска́ти (zyskáty).
From Old Ruthenian кре́йда, креида (kréjda, kreida), from Middle Polish krejda, from Middle High German krīde, from Old High German krīda, from Latin crēta.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ки́лька (kílʹka), from Middle Polish kilka, from Old Polish kilko, kielko, from Proto-Slavic *koliko. Doublet of кі́лько, кі́льки (kílʹko, kílʹky, “how many, how much”).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian ко́лкость (kólkostʹ), probably a calque of Middle Polish ilość, ultimately a calque of Latin quantitās, which is a calque of Ancient Greek ποσότης (posótēs). By surface analysis, кі́лько (kílʹko, “how much, how many”) + -ість (-istʹ). Compare Old Church Slavonic количьст
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ліосъ (lios), borrowed from Middle Polish los. Doublet of лото́ (lotó).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian мо́жна (móžna), from Middle Polish można, ellipsis of (jest) rzecz można, literally, “[the] thing (is) possible”.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian нагоро́да (nahoróda), borrowed from Middle Polish nagroda in XVI (whence also Old Ruthenian нагро́да (nahróda)), remodeled after native pleophonic forms, such as городъ, городити (horod, horoditi).

parole.significato: pile, stilt, pier (a beam, pole, or pillar, driven completely into the ground, usually as one of a group that constitut…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian палꙗ (palja), borrowed from Middle Polish pal.

parole.significato: to pursue, to chase, to hunt
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian переслѣдовати (pereslědovati), from earlier Old Ruthenian преслѣдовати (preslědovati), most likely from Middle Polish prześladować, ultimately a calque of Latin persequor and/or prosequor. By surface analysis, пере- (pere-) + слі́дувати (slíduvaty).

parole.significato: to pull up, to hitch up, to tuck up, to tuck in, to roll up (clothes: sleeves, pants, skirt, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian подкасати (podkasati), from Middle Polish podkasać. By surface analysis, під- (pid-) + -каса́ти (-kasáty).

parole.significato: to care (for), to take care of, to look after (про + accusative, ко́ло + genitive)
parole.testo: From earlier пеклува́тися (pekluvátysja), from Old Ruthenian пеклова́тисꙗ (peklovátisja, “to care about, to take care of”), from Middle Polish piekłować się. By surface analysis, пе́кло (péklo) + -ува́ти (-uváty) + -ся (-sja). For the semantic variety compare Polish pieklić się (“to be angry”), dial

parole.significato: to rob, to steal from, to plunder, to pillage
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian рабова́ти (rabováti), from Middle Polish rabować, from Middle High German rouben, from Old High German roubōn, from Proto-West Germanic *raubōn, from Proto-Germanic *raubōną, whence also English rob and reave.
Borrowed from Middle Polish ratować.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian тлумъ (tlum), from Middle Polish tłum, from Proto-Slavic *tъlpa + *-mъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian *трꙋтити (*trutiti), judging by the geography, possibly from Middle Polish trącić, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *trǫtiti.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian трꙋчати (tručati), judging by the geography, possibly from Middle Polish trącać. By surface analysis, тру́тити (trútyty) + -я́ти (-játy).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian тꙋрбаціꙗ (turbacija), from Middle Polish turbacja, from Latin turbātiō.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian черво́ный (červónyj), from Middle Polish czerwony, from Old Polish czerwiony with the depalatalization of 'w' under the Czech influence, from Proto-Slavic *čьrvenъ or *čьrvľenъ, past passive participle of *čьrviti (“to dye red”). Doublet of native червле́ний and черве́ни
Inherited from Old Ruthenian истота (istota), from Middle Polish istota, from Old Polish istota, from isty + -ota.
